result.effect: IFG positive-versus-neutral face prediction AUC increase=0.134, permutation p=0.047

cells.quote: Moreover, 10,000 times permutation tests showed that the accuracy of using the IFG as a restriction region for predicting positive and neutral expression faces was signiﬁcantly higher in the post-FISL than inthe pre-FISL session (increase in AUC: 0.134, permutation test p = 0.047).
cells.note: This is the reported long-term transfer effect to emotional-face perception after the month-long FISL course.

O.outcome_detail: number-noun pairs episodic-memory accuracy after training

cells.quote: After applying false-discovery-rate (FDR) corrections to all resulting p values, we observed a signi ﬁcant interaction effect on the number-noun pairs measure, suggesting that the MT group performed better on this test compared to the NC group after undergoing training and the improvement persisted over time as seen in the follow-up (Table 1).
cells.note: The study reports the significant Group × Session interaction but does not print an effect size for the number-noun pairs contrast.

cells.quote: After applying false-discovery-rate (FDR) corrections to all resulting p values, we observed a signi ﬁcant interaction effect on the number-noun pairs measure, suggesting that the MT group performed better on this test compared to the NC group after undergoing training and the improvement persisted over time as seen in the follow-up (Table 1).
cells.note: The follow-up occurred 4 months after training; the study states that the improvement persisted but does not print a separate follow-up effect size.

cells.quote:
It revealed the signi ﬁcance only for the Group × Session interaction, F (1, 31) = 15.46, p < 0.001, η2

Upon further analysis, it was found that post-training discriminability (M ± SE, 2.10 ± 0.19) was signi ﬁcantly higher than pre-training discriminability in the MT group (1.37 ± 0.12), p < 0.001. O.outcome_detail: P200 amplitude for even- versus odd-position digits during encoding

cells.quote:
More importantly, we found the interaction effect of Position × Session, F (1, 15) = 3.79, p < 0.05, η2
partial = 0.17: the post-training session showed greater P200 amplitude in response to even-position digits (3.08 ± 0.96 μV) compared to odd-position digits (1.34 ± 0.80 μV), p < 0.05 (Fig. 4). No other main effect or interaction was signiﬁcant. As a control, in the NC group, there was no such P200 effect, as indicated by the lack of signiﬁcance for the effects involving Session or Position, all ps > 0.41.
cells.note: The neural contrast is the post-training even-versus-odd encoding pattern, absent in the no-contact control group.

O.outcome_detail: left-anterior theta power for even- versus odd-position digits during encoding

result.effect: F(2, 30) = 6.92, p < 0.05, η2 partial = 0.37; post-training Position × Area F(2, 30) = 14.43, p < 0.01, η2 partial = 0.55

cells.quote: Further analysis showed that the post-training session demonstrated a signiﬁcant increase in theta power from the odd- (10 ± 5 %, percent signal change) to even-position (24 ± 6 %) condition in the left anterior area, p < 0.05 (Fig. 5), but the pre-training session did not. No other main effect or interaction was signiﬁcant. In the NC group, the three-way ANOVA found no signiﬁcant results, all ps > 0.09.
cells.note: The reported effect is a training-induced odd-even theta pattern during encoding.

O.outcome_detail: number-noun pairs memory, including four-month follow-up

cells.quote: After applying false-discovery-rate (FDR) corrections to all resulting p values, we observed a signi ﬁcant interaction effect on the number-noun pairs measure, suggesting that the MT group performed better on this test compared to the NC group after undergoing training and the improvement persisted over time as seen in the follow-up (Table 1). No other signi ﬁcant interaction effects were observed.
cells.note: The study describes this as limited enhancement in assessed cognitive abilities; no numerical effect size for the interaction is reported.
